topic: Why most college essays fail and what actually makes students stand out
student_profile: General high school applicant writing Common App or supplemental essays. No individual student profile — public advising content.
problem: Most essays sound the same: students think they need a dramatic story (surviving cancer, losing a loved one) to stand out, but generic dramatic stories actually blend together.
advice_given: Colleges do not admit students because of what happened to them — they admit students because of how they think and who they are.
Extraordinary events written generically lose impact. Ordinary events written with genuine insight can be extraordinary.
Avoid "this experience taught me" summary endings — they flatten the essay.
Specific, concrete details beat dramatic events every time.
The best essays show a distinctive way of seeing the world, not just a touching story.
Readers can spot essays written to impress rather than to reveal.
reasoning: After reading 100 essays, pattern is clear: topic matters far less than voice, specificity, and insight. Students selecting big dramatic topics often produce the most formulaic essays because they rely on event weight instead of perspective.
action_plan: Pick a topic you can write about with genuine specificity — not the most impressive topic.
Write a draft, then highlight every sentence that could have been written by any other student. Delete or rewrite all of them.
Replace summary statements with concrete scenes, details, sensory description.
Ask a reader: after this essay, what do you know about me that you didn't before? If answer is vague, revise.
Test ending: does it add meaning or just re-state the lesson already shown?
risks: Avoiding dramatic topics is not the goal — avoiding generic treatment is.
Over-correcting toward "ordinary topic" without strong voice still produces weak essays.
Advice is craft-level; does not address school-specific supplemental strategy.
creator: YouTube: What 100 college essays taught me about who gets rejected
